steps.text: By the end you can explain how the queen moves, what stops her, and how a queen is trapped or lost in three moves. First, try a position cold: tap every square she can reach.

That was the **queen**: a rook and a bishop in one piece. She has **eight lines**, four straight and four slanting, and she slides along each over empty squares, as far as she likes. Not sure how you did? Good. The next boards are a worked example, so look first, then try again.

steps.caption: The piece on c3 is a queen. Her pawn on e3 and king on e1 stop two lines one square early. The knight on d5 is on none of her lines (it does attack her, which is the next chapter).

line.say: The queen slides up and to the left along a diagonal, over empty squares, to a5.
Black moves the king; we are only watching the queen.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on c3 can move to.

steps.caption: This is the position you tried. Seven lines are open, 24 squares in all. White's own pawn on f3 shuts the eighth line at once.

line.say: She glides up and to the left, over empty squares, as far as b7.
Black's king steps aside again.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on e4 can move to.

steps.caption: From a1 she reaches 21 squares; from d4 on an empty board 27, because all eight lines run across the board. A corner costs her few squares but five of her eight lines.

line.say: She steps to the middle: now all eight lines run across the board.
Black's king moves; the queen is the one being studied.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on a1 can move to.

steps.text: Every line ends by itself. An **own piece** is a wall: she stops on the square before it. An **enemy piece** is the last square of the line: she may take it, and then she stops there. She never hops over either kind. Watch both on the next two boards.

steps.caption: Her own pawn closes the long diagonal at d4. The other lines from a1 stay open.

line.say: She slides along the diagonal and stops one square before her own pawn.
Black's king moves; nothing else changes.

claims.statement: Her own pawn stands on d4.
She cannot hop over her own pawn.
The file upward is still open.
The first rank is still open.

steps.caption: An enemy pawn on d4 is the last square of that diagonal. She may take it, but not go past it.

line.say: She captures the pawn and stops on its square.
Black's king steps aside.

claims.statement: The pawn on d4 ends the line, so e5 is out of reach.

steps.text: A blocker closes **one** line; the other seven stay open unless she is pinned or her king is in check (both come later). So when a piece stands next to her, count the lines again, one by one. *Rule of thumb:* eight lines, each checked on its own.

steps.caption: A white pawn on c4 shuts the line straight up. Look at what is still open: seven lines, 20 squares.

line.say: The diagonal toward e5 is as open as it ever was.
Black's king steps aside.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen on c3 can move to.
Her own pawn on c4 is in the way.

steps.caption: A lone queen can use all three kinds of slide. Here she makes one of each, and the kings stay out of the way.

line.say: Straight up the file, like a rook.
Black's king steps aside.
Straight along the rank, also like a rook.
Black's king steps again.
Along a diagonal, like a bishop: the third kind of slide.

claims.statement: e3 is on none of her lines.

steps.caption: From d4 the square e6 is a knight's jump away: one file across and two ranks up. The queen needs two moves to get there.

line.say: One slide along a diagonal: now e6 is straight above her.
Black's king steps aside.
A second slide up the file reaches e6. One move could not.

claims.statement: A knight's jump is not a line.

steps.title: Lines, jumps, blockers
steps.prompt: Predict first. The first position asks for every square. The second asks one yes/no question about a square a knight could reach from the same square. In the third, a pawn moved next to the queen: which of the queen's other lines are still open?

steps.text: There is a trap here. A piece can stand *on her line* and still be out of reach, when another piece stands between. She sees only up to the first piece on each line. So ask two questions: is it on one of my lines, and is every square between us empty?

steps.caption: The rook on h8 is on the queen's long diagonal, but the pawn on d4 stands between. She can take the pawn, never the rook.

line.say: She takes the first piece on the line.
The diagonal is now open, but the king guards the rook, so taking it would lose her. Ask: is the square guarded?

claims.statement: The pawn on d4 stands in the way.

steps.text: The queen is worth the most of any piece but the king: about nine pawns on the counting scale (a rule of thumb, not a law). So usually she should not take a pawn that a pawn can take back, unless the capture mates or wins more than the queen. [I] Before every capture ask one question: **does anything of theirs guard that square?**

steps.caption: The black knight on d6 is loose: nothing of Black's guards it. The queen sees it straight up the open file.

line.say: She takes the knight and nothing can take her back.
Black's king steps aside, a knight down.

steps.caption: The same slide, but now a pawn on c6 guards the pawn on d5. Taking it would cost the queen.

line.say: The queen takes a pawn along the open file.
But the pawn on c6 guards that square and takes her: nine points lost for one.

steps.caption: The pawn on e5 attacks the queen, and a pawn on d6 guards that pawn. Taking it would lose her, so she steps to a square no black piece attacks.

line.say: She moves along the file to d3, out of the pawn's reach.
Black's king steps aside; the queen is safe.

steps.caption: The black knight on b5 attacks the queen, but she cannot attack it: b5 is not on any of her lines. Knights attack by jumping.

line.say: She slips away along the file, to a square the knight does not attack.
Black's king steps aside.

claims.statement: A knight's square is not on her lines.

steps.text: [H] A guess, not a measured fact: when the queen comes out early, every piece that attacks her gains a free move, because she has to run. Test it: in the pawn-attack line below, count the moves each side made. The next three boards show one famous example.

steps.caption: White brings the queen out on move two, aiming along a diagonal at f7. [I] f7 is guarded only by the king at the start, which is why beginners often aim here. A bishop will help.

line.say: The queen glides up the diagonal to h5, in sight of the pawn on f7.
Black develops a knight and does not defend f7.
The bishop also aims at f7: now two white pieces attack it.

steps.caption: Black develops a knight, but it blocks nothing and leaves f7 guarded only by the king.

line.say: The queen takes on f7, guarded by the bishop, and it is checkmate.

steps.caption: Black has a better answer: a pawn move that attacks the queen. A pawn is worth one point and the queen nine, so she must run.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen, and it also closes her diagonal.
The queen retreats. White has used two queen moves, while Black made useful moves with a pawn and a knight. [H] Early queen moves can cost tempi.

steps.text: The lesson of the three boards, and a rule of thumb: the queen is at her best once other pieces help her and few enemy pieces can hit her. [I] My inference from these boards: develop other pieces first, so the queen is not the first piece attacked. Judge each early queen move by one question: who can attack her next?

steps.caption: Here White's king is in check from the rook on e8. A queen move now has one job: end the check. Three squares do it.

line.say: She takes the rook that gives check, along the diagonal.
Her capture also gives check, so Black's king must move.

claims.statement: These are exactly the squares the queen can move to.

steps.caption: Her lines can also end the game. The black king is boxed in by its own pawns, and the d-file is open.

line.say: One long slide to the last rank: check, and no flight square, so it is checkmate.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend who has never seen the queen: how she moves, what stops her, and what to ask before she takes something. Write 2-3 sentences.

steps.text: **Compare with your answer.** A model: the queen has eight lines, four straight and four slanting. Each line ends before her own piece or on the first enemy piece, and a blocker closes only its own line. She never jumps. Before a capture, ask: is that square guarded?

steps.prompt: In the silent items, which of the eight lines did you check last? Which one did you most often forget to check?
